summary: This standards-track document defines a YANG data model for Layer 3 network topologies. It extends the generic network topology model so that IP-level nodes, links and attributes can be described in a standard way.

eli5.summary: A basic map shows towns and roads. This adds the street addresses that matter for the internet's own routing level.

questions: what is the yang model for layer 3 topology
how to represent an ip topology in yang
subtitle: A standard YANG model for describing Layer 3 network topologies: nodes, links, prefixes and interfaces.

tldr.problem: Applications and controllers need a standard, holistic way to represent the topology of a Layer 3 network in a single conceptual datastore.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-l3-unicast-topology YANG module augments the generic network topology model of RFC 8345 with Layer 3 Unicast attributes for networks, nodes, links and termination points, plus notifications for changes.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators and tools a common schema that can be refined for specific topology types, with an OSPF example in an appendix. A companion module serves implementations without NMDA support.

today: RFC 8346 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8345.

sections.title: What the Model Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8346 defines a YANG data model for Layer 3 (L3) network topologies, specifically Layer 3 Unicast. The model lets an application see the topology of an L3 network as a whole, all held in one conceptual datastore. It builds on, and augments, the generic network topology model of RFC 8345.

The RFC gives example uses. Nodes can record their understanding of the topology and expose it to a network controller, which can compare and reconcile that against its own view. Nodes could also compare their views with each other. A controller might even use the model to present the topology it controls to applications above it.

Information kept in the Traffic Engineering Database is out of scope and left to a separate model. The OSPF content in the appendix is only an illustration, and the RFC expects a complete OSPF model to be more comprehensive.
sections.eli5: Imagine every router could describe the network map in the same words. Then a helper program can read all the maps and spot where they disagree.

sections.title: Model Structure and NMDA
sections.content:
The model is the YANG module ietf-l3-unicast-topology. The modules ietf-network and ietf-network-topology from RFC 8345 define the basic topology. The L3 module augments them, and other modules can in turn augment the L3 module for specific topology types, such as OSPF and IS-IS.

The base modules are designed for implementations that support the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342, and so does everything that augments them. For implementations without NMDA, Appendix A defines a companion module, ietf-l3-unicast-topology-state. It mirrors the main module, but augments the matching state modules and all its data nodes are non-configurable. Implementations that support NMDA SHOULD NOT support the companion module.
sections.eli5: The new module is a sticker sheet for an existing map. The basic map stays as it is, and the stickers add layer-3 details on top.

sections.title: What the Module Adds
sections.content:
The module augments the base model in five places, all described with the tree notation of RFC 8340.

  • Network type: a new topology type, l3-unicast-topology, marks a network as L3 Unicast.
  • Topology: l3-topology-attributes has a name and a set of flags.
  • Nodes: l3-node-attributes has a name, flags, router IDs and a list of prefixes. Each prefix has an IP prefix, a metric and its own flags.
  • Links: l3-link-attributes has a name, flags and two metrics, metric1 and metric2.
  • Termination points: l3-termination-point-attributes offers a choice of IP addresses, an unnumbered-interface identifier or an interface name.

Flags are a leaf-list of identities, so augmenting modules can add new flag types without changing this module. The unnumbered identifier corresponds to the ifIndex value of the interface where the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863) is supported.
sections.eli5: The map's cities (nodes), roads (links) and doors into the cities (termination points) each get extra labels, like a name, a cost to travel, and an address.

sections.title: Change Notifications
sections.content:
The module also defines notifications that tell clients about events on nodes, links, prefixes and termination points: l3-node-event, l3-link-event, l3-prefix-event and termination-point-event. Each carries an event type of add, remove or update, the topology it came from and the affected object.

Notifications also include additional data of the affected object. The RFC admits this makes them larger than necessary, but it saves the client from fetching context that might have changed in the meantime.
sections.eli5: When something on the map changes, the model sends a note saying what was added, removed or changed, and includes the details so you do not have to look it up again.

sections.title: Fit With Other YANG Modules
sections.content:
The L3 module augments ietf-network and ietf-network-topology and uses data types from RFC 6991. It imports one type from ietf-routing-types (RFC 8294).

It is a protocol-independent model of Layer 3 topology information. It is separate from, and not linked to, models that configure routing protocols or routing information, such as ietf-routing (RFC 8022).

The model complies with the requirements for ephemeral state in RFC 8242. For server-provided ephemeral topology data, the process that maintains it loads information from the routing process (such as OSPF) into the model without relying on a configuration datastore.
sections.eli5: This model only describes the map. It does not tell routers how to behave, so it sits beside the other models rather than replacing them.

sections.title: Extending It: An OSPF Example
sections.content:
Appendix B shows how the model can be refined with a simple example module, example-ospf-topology. It is explicitly an example and is not normative; it does not define how to configure OSPF routers or interfaces.

The example adds an ospf topology type, an area-id in the topology attributes, a router type for nodes and, for pseudonodes, a dr-interface-id. The router type is a choice of abr, asbr, internal or pseudonode. Links get an OSPF attribute container, and node and link notifications are extended with the OSPF attributes.
sections.eli5: It shows how you could add stickers just for one kind of road network, like marking a boss router or an area, without redrawing the whole map.

sections.title: A Worked Topology Example
sections.content:
Appendix C gives an instance in JSON encoding of a network with three nodes, D1, D2 and D3. D1 has termination points 1-0-1, 1-2-1 and 1-3-1, D2 has 2-1-1, 2-0-1 and 2-3-1, and D3 has 3-1-1 and 3-2-1. There are six links, two between each pair of nodes, one in each direction.

The nodes carry router IDs 203.0.113.1, 203.0.113.2 and 203.0.113.3. The termination points use unnumbered IDs such as 101 and 121, and the links shown carry a metric1 of 100.
sections.eli5: Three towns, each pair joined by two one-way roads, one for each direction. Every road has a toll of 100.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The schema is meant to be accessed with management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. The NETCONF access control model (RFC 8341) can limit which users see or change which parts of the data.

L3 Unicast topologies are system-controlled and ephemeral. In an NMDA-compliant server they appear only in the operational datastore, which is read-only for clients, so they are less vulnerable. The modules do allow writable data in principle, and unprotected writes could hurt network operations.

The RFC names the sensitive subtrees: l3-topology-attributes, l3-node-attributes (for example router-id or node prefix), l3-link-attributes (name, flag and metrics) and l3-termination-point-attributes (IP address and interface name). In each case a malicious client could try to sabotage the configuration.
sections.eli5: The map is normally read-only, but if someone could scribble on it, routers might get sent the wrong way. So only trusted people should be allowed to write on it.
